findings.source_passage: all mortal greatness is but disease. But, as yet we have not to do with such an one, but with quite another
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'And when these things unite in a man of greatly superior natural force'
findings.why_it_matters: 'All mortal greatness is but disease' is one of Moby-Dick's most quoted and critically engaged aphorisms; the entire paragraph is a primary interpretive key to Ahab and the novel's tragic framework, anticipating everything that follows. Its absence removes the conceptual scaffolding Melville places here deliberately.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full paragraph from 'And when these things unite in a man of greatly superior natural force' through 'all mortal greatness is but disease' — at minimum preserve the aphorism verbatim and the globular-brain/ponderous-heart characterization that grounds the Ahab archetype.

findings.source_passage: I _dost_, said I unconsciously, he was so intense a Quaker.
findings.source_locator: dialogue exchange between Peleg, Bildad, and Ishmael after signing articles
findings.why_it_matters: This is a characteristic Ishmaelian comedic aside — the narrator's involuntary grammatical contagion — that establishes the voice's self-deprecating irony and the comic texture of the Bildad scenes; its loss flattens the register.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the brief 'I dost, said I unconsciously, he was so intense a Quaker' exchange; it requires only one line and is a signature voice moment.

findings.source_passage: I am one of those that never take on about princely fortunes, and am quite content if the world is ready to board and lodge me, while I am putting up at this grim sign of the Thunder Cloud.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'It might be thought that this was a poor way to accumulate a princely fortune'
findings.why_it_matters: This is voice-establishing Ishmael — his self-characterizing digression on ambition and contentment is one of the narrator's defining tonal signatures in this chapter, and 'the grim sign of the Thunder Cloud' is a distinctively Melvillean flourish that marks the narrator's ironic stoicism.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the brief paragraph including the 'Thunder Cloud' line; it is short and carries high voice-density.

findings.source_passage: I felt a sympathy and a sorrow for him, but for I don't know what... that sort of awe, which I cannot at all describe, was not exactly awe; I do not know what it was. But I felt it
findings.why_it_matters: The closing paragraph's recursive, groping syntax — 'not exactly awe; I do not know what it was. But I felt it' — is critically noted as Ishmael's signature mode of epistemological confession; the draft compresses it to 'not exactly awe—possessed me' and loses the deliberate self-interrupting rhythm.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the verbatim closing rhythm: 'that sort of awe, which I cannot at all describe, was not exactly awe; I do not know what it was. But I felt it' — these phrases are the chapter's final voice-signature and should not be smoothed.

summary: The draft's most serious failure is the complete erasure of the 'all mortal greatness is but disease' paragraph — an interpretive keystone and the chapter's most-quoted critical passage — compounded by three medium-severity voice losses that strip Ishmael's comic and epistemological register from the chapter's frame.
